newsitem.title: USA: S&P sticks to B rating on DC, despite Clinton plan.
newsitem.headline: S&P sticks to B rating on DC, despite Clinton plan.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Rating Services said it is sticking with its junk 'B' rating for District of Columbia bonds despite President Clinton's upcoming $3.9 billion relief package for the financially stressed city.
S&P said in its weekly municipal credits report that Clinton's proposal, due out February 4, "could lead to improved credit quality for the District."

But the plan must endure a lengthy approval process on Capitol Hill, which means it is too soon to tell what the final version will be, said S&P, which also has given D.C.'s rating a stable outlook. The 'B' rating is on city general obligation bonds.

The President's plan provides for $885 million in capital spending on prison renovations and construction; $891 million to operate prison facilities; $681 million to operate the city's court system; $125 million, beginning in 1998, to rebuild transportation infrastruture; $117 million to improve city tax collections; and $917 million to increase the federal government's share of Medicaid payments.
The net cost to the federal government would be $339 million over five years, because the plan would wipe out the District's current $660 million appropriation from Congress, S&P said.
